Cue is an event within a visuospatial working-memory task; the contrast is a task-related main effect (WM cue > control) and so meets pooled executive-function inclusion (WM is one of the six domains and the contrast reflects task-related executive demand).

The Cue event is an encoding/encoding-related main effect from a visuospatial working-memory paradigm (WM cue > control), so it meets working-memory inclusion (task is WM and contrast isolates encoding/maintenance-related activity).
Cue presentation does not come from a canonical inhibition paradigm (e.g., Go/No-Go, Stroop); the contrast isolates encoding/visual WM cue activity rather than inhibitory demand.
Cue activity does not reflect a task-switching/set-shifting paradigm or switching demand; it is an encoding/cue main effect.
This contrast is not a Tower-style planning task or planning-demand contrast; it indexes cue/encoding in a WM task.
The cue event is not an oddball/target-detection vigilance paradigm nor a target>standard contrast; it reflects WM cue encoding instead.
The contrast does not index self-initiated generation (word generation/fluency); it is a cue/encoding event in a WM task.

Delay is the maintenance phase of a visuospatial working-memory task and the contrast is a task-related main effect (WM delay > control), satisfying pooled executive-function inclusion (WM domain and task-related demand).
Delay-related activity is a canonical working-memory maintenance contrast (WM delay > control); meets working-memory criteria (WM paradigm and delay/maintenance contrast).
The delay contrast indexes maintenance in WM rather than a response-inhibition paradigm; it does not meet inhibition-task criteria.
Delay activity is not a task-switching/set-shifting contrast and therefore fails cognitive-flexibility inclusion.
This is a WM maintenance contrast, not a Tower-style planning contrast.
Delay-related WM maintenance is not an oddball/target-detection vigilance contrast.
The contrast does not index self-initiated generation/fluency; it reflects maintenance during WM delay.

Distraction contrasts (distraction > WM delay) probe executive aspects of ignoring interference during a WM task; WM is one of the six executive domains and the contrast isolates task-related executive demand (distractor processing/ignoring), so pooled executive-function inclusion applies.

The distraction contrast isolates distracter-evoked processing (distraction > delay) rather than maintenance/manipulation/load per se, so it does not meet the working-memory inclusion (maintenance/load/encoding) and is excluded.

Although distraction relates to resisting interference, the contrast is not from a canonical inhibition paradigm (Go/No-Go, Stroop) and therefore does not meet the strict inhibition inclusion criteria.
This contrast does not index switching/set-shifting (task-switch) demands, so cognitive-flexibility criteria are not met.
Distraction-versus-delay is not a planning (Tower) contrast and thus fails planning inclusion.
Distraction here isolates distracter responses during WM rather than target>standard vigilance/oddball detection contrasts, so it does not meet vigilance inclusion.
The distraction contrast does not index self-initiated generation/fluency and therefore fails initiation inclusion.

Selection (response selection) is part of the WM task where maintained information is used to guide responses; the contrast is task-related and thus satisfies pooled executive-function inclusion (WM domain, task demand).

The Selection event reflects using maintained information to guide response selection (WM retrieval/use), matching the working-memory definition and inclusion (WM paradigm and use to guide response selection).
Selection contrasts here index response-selection in WM rather than canonical inhibition paradigms (No-Go/Stroop), so inhibition criteria are not met.
This is not a task-switching/set-shifting contrast; it indexes response selection, so cognitive-flexibility is not applicable.
Selection does not reflect Tower-style planning demands; planning inclusion is not met.
Selection is a response/choice event, not an oddball/target-detection vigilance contrast.
The contrast does not index self-initiated generation/fluency, so initiation criteria are unmet.
This (second-table) Cue main effect again indexes WM cue/encoding within the visuospatial WM task (within-group main effect), so pooled executive-function inclusion applies.
Cue is an encoding-related main effect from a WM paradigm (meets WM inclusion for encoding/maintenance/use).
Cue activity does not reflect canonical inhibition paradigms; it indexes WM cue/encoding.
Cue is not a switching/set-shifting contrast; cognitive-flexibility criteria are not met.
This contrast is not a planning (Tower) task contrast.
Cue event is not an oddball/target-detection vigilance contrast.
Cue does not index self-initiated generation/fluency.

Delay is a canonical working-memory maintenance contrast (WM delay > control) and therefore meets working-memory inclusion.

The contrast does not index self-initiated generation/fluency.

This selection contrast reflects response selection within WM rather than inhibition in a Go/No-Go or Stroop sense, so it does not meet inhibition criteria.

Selection does not index Tower-style planning demands.
This contrast is not an oddball/target-detection vigilance contrast.

Analysis ‘spatial recall’ is a within-group, whole-brain task activation contrast probing recall of spatial relations held online (an executive working-memory demand). The task falls within the six EF domains (working memory) and the contrast is a main effect of that task vs baseline, meeting both global and local inclusion criteria.

This analysis examines maintenance/retrieval of spatial relations from a recently viewed scene (delayed recall), matching the working memory paradigm requirement; the contrast is a main effect of the recall task versus baseline/other conditions, satisfying working-memory inclusion criteria.
The contrast is a spatial working-memory recall task, not an inhibition paradigm (e.g. Go/No-Go, Stroop). It does not isolate inhibitory demands.
This is not a task-switching/set-shifting contrast (no switch>repeat or set-shift manipulation); it instead probes recall within working memory and so does not meet flexibility criteria.
The task is a spatial recall/working-memory task rather than a planning paradigm (Tower-type); it does not meet planning criteria.
This is not an oddball/target-detection or sustained vigilance paradigm; the contrast does not index set-maintenance in the vigilance sense.
The task does not involve self-initiated generation (e.g. verbal fluency); it is a cued recall task and thus does not meet initiation criteria.

‘Allocentric spatial recall > egocentric spatial recall’ is a within-group, whole-brain contrast probing differing executive demands within spatial working memory (frame-of-reference shift). The task falls under the executive-function umbrella (working memory domain) and the contrast indexes executive demand differences, meeting pooled-EF inclusion criteria.

Both allocentric and egocentric conditions are spatial working-memory recall; the contrast isolates differential working-memory demands (shifting/transforming the representation). This fits WORKING_MEMORY_I1/I2.
This contrast does not test response inhibition (e.g. No-Go vs Go or incongruent vs congruent); it isolates differences within spatial recall instead.

Although allocentric>egocentric involves changing reference frames, the local inclusion requires explicit task-switching/set-shifting contrasts (switch>repeat). This contrast does not implement a conventional flexibility paradigm and therefore fails the flexibility inclusion criteria.
The contrast targets spatial recall/frame transformation rather than planning operations (Tower tasks); it does not meet planning inclusion.
This is not a vigilance/oddball or sustained target-detection contrast; it does not probe set-maintenance under interference as defined for vigilance.
The contrast does not involve self-initiated generation (word/fluency tasks). It is a cued recall contrast and therefore does not meet initiation criteria.

‘Allocentric spatial recall > baseline’ is a within-group, whole-brain main-effect contrast of a spatial working-memory recall condition (allocentric), which is within the executive-function domains (working memory). The contrast reflects task executive demand vs baseline, meeting pooled-EF inclusion criteria.

Allocentric recall vs baseline is an encoding/maintenance/retrieval main effect of a spatial working-memory task (delayed recall), satisfying working-memory inclusion criteria for a main-effect contrast of WM.
This contrast does not test inhibitory control paradigms (No-Go, Stroop, antisaccade) and thus does not meet inhibition criteria.
This is a main-effect WM contrast (allocentric recall) not a task-switch/set-shift contrast; it does not meet the flexibility inclusion requirements.
Allocentric recall is not a planning (Tower-type) task and therefore fails planning inclusion criteria.
This is not a vigilance/oddball or target-detection contrast and does not index sustained-set maintenance under interference as required for vigilance.
The contrast does not involve self-initiated generation (verbal fluency) and thus does not meet initiation criteria.

‘Performance vs. AlloSpace–EgoSpace’ is a within-group, whole-brain regression linking behavioral performance to the allocentric>egocentric working-memory contrast. It probes executive-function variation (working-memory-related) across subjects and so meets pooled-EF inclusion criteria.

This analysis examines the relationship between performance on spatial recall tasks and the AlloSpace–EgoSpace contrast (both are working-memory conditions). The regression links WM-related activation to behavioral WM performance, satisfying WORKING_MEMORY_I1/I2.
The analysis is a performance correlation of a spatial recall contrast, not an inhibition paradigm, so it does not meet inhibition inclusion criteria.

Although the contrast involves allocentric vs egocentric frames, the analysis is not a canonical task-switch/set-shifting contrast (switch>repeat); it therefore does not meet flexibility inclusion criteria.
This is a WM performance correlation, not a planning (Tower-type) contrast, so it does not meet planning criteria.
This regression analysis is not an oddball/target-detection or sustained vigilance contrast and thus does not meet vigilance inclusion criteria.
This analysis does not index self-initiated generation (e.g. verbal fluency); it is a performance correlation on a cued recall WM contrast and therefore fails initiation criteria.

This is a within-group, whole-brain contrast of the Sternberg working memory task (average encoding across loads). WM is one of the six executive domains and the contrast is a main effect of task vs implicit baseline, meeting pooled EF criteria.
The analysis is an encoding main-effect contrast from a Sternberg working memory paradigm (within-group, whole-brain), so it meets both the task-type and contrast-type WM inclusion criteria.
This contrast isolates working memory encoding (Sternberg task) rather than an inhibition paradigm; it does not meet inhibition inclusion and therefore is excluded.
This contrast isolates working memory encoding (Sternberg task) rather than a task-switching/set-shifting paradigm; it does not meet flexibility inclusion and therefore is excluded.
This contrast is from a Sternberg working memory task, not a Tower-type planning paradigm, so it does not meet planning inclusion and is excluded.
This is a working memory encoding contrast, not an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast; it does not meet vigilance inclusion and is excluded.
The contrast reflects Sternberg working memory encoding rather than word-generation/self-initiation paradigms; it does not meet initiation inclusion and is excluded.

This analysis is a linear regression with memory load in the Sternberg working memory task (within-group, whole-brain). Load-dependent WM is an executive demand and therefore counts toward pooled executive function.
The contrast is a linear regression on memory load in a Sternberg working memory paradigm, directly matching WM inclusion criteria (task type and load effect).
This is a WM load regression contrast, not an inhibition paradigm; it does not meet inhibition inclusion and is excluded.
This contrast assesses load in a Sternberg WM task rather than task-switching; it does not meet flexibility inclusion and is excluded.
This is a WM load contrast, not a planning (Tower) task contrast; it does not meet planning inclusion and is excluded.
This is a working memory load regression, not an oddball/vigilance contrast; it does not meet vigilance inclusion and is excluded.
This is a Sternberg WM load regression, not a word-generation/self-initiation contrast; it does not meet initiation inclusion and is excluded.

This is a within-group, whole-brain contrast of the maintenance (delay) phase in the Sternberg working memory task (average maintenance vs baseline). Maintenance is an executive function domain included in pooled EF and the contrast is a main effect.
The analysis is the maintenance (delay) main-effect contrast from a Sternberg working memory paradigm, directly meeting WM inclusion criteria for maintenance-related contrasts.
This contrast isolates maintenance in a WM task rather than an inhibition paradigm; it does not meet inhibition inclusion and is excluded.
This is a delay/maintenance contrast from a Sternberg WM task, not a task-switching/set-shifting contrast; it does not meet flexibility inclusion and is excluded.
This is a maintenance-phase WM contrast, not a planning (Tower) paradigm contrast; it does not meet planning inclusion and is excluded.

Although maintenance involves sustained maintenance, this analysis is framed as the delay main effect in a Sternberg WM task rather than an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast; thus it does not meet the specified vigilance inclusion and is excluded.
This contrast reflects maintenance in a Sternberg WM task, not self-initiated word-generation; it does not meet initiation inclusion and is excluded.
This is a within-group, whole-brain contrast of retrieval (average across loads) in the Sternberg working memory task. Retrieval/main-effect WM contrasts are executive and count toward pooled EF.
The analysis is the retrieval main-effect contrast from the Sternberg working memory paradigm, satisfying WM task-type and contrast-type inclusion criteria.
This contrast isolates retrieval in a Sternberg WM task rather than an inhibition paradigm; it does not meet inhibition inclusion and is excluded.
This is a WM retrieval contrast, not a task-switching/set-shifting contrast, so it does not meet flexibility inclusion and is excluded.
This retrieval contrast derives from a Sternberg WM task rather than a Tower planning paradigm and therefore does not meet planning inclusion.
This is a WM retrieval main-effect contrast, not an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast; it does not meet vigilance inclusion and is excluded.
This contrast reflects retrieval in a Sternberg WM task, not self-initiated verbal generation; it does not meet initiation inclusion and is excluded.

This analysis is a linear regression of retrieval activity with memory load in the Sternberg working memory task (within-group, whole-brain). Load-dependent retrieval reflects executive demand and is included in pooled EF.
The contrast is a linear regression on memory load during retrieval in the Sternberg working memory paradigm, directly matching WM inclusion criteria for load effects and retrieval.
This is a WM load regression during retrieval, not an inhibition (No-Go/Stroop) contrast; it does not meet inhibition inclusion and is excluded.
This contrast assesses load in a Sternberg WM retrieval phase rather than task-switching; it does not meet flexibility inclusion and is excluded.
This is a retrieval load regression from a Sternberg WM task, not a planning (Tower) contrast, so it does not meet planning inclusion and is excluded.
This is a WM retrieval load regression, not an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast; it does not meet vigilance inclusion and is excluded.
This contrast reflects load-dependent retrieval in a Sternberg WM task, not a word-generation/self-initiation contrast; it does not meet initiation inclusion and is excluded.

Contrast IG-PRE vs EG-PRE isolates premovement planning/maintenance and sequence complexity effects (executive demands). Global within-group whole-brain task contrast criteria met.

IG premovement involves maintaining sequence information across a delay (memory maintenance); the contrast compares informative (IG) premovement vs uninformative (EG) premovement, meeting WM inclusion criteria.
This contrast is a motor sequencing/maintenance contrast, not an inhibition paradigm (e.g. Go/No-Go, Stroop); therefore it isolates a different domain.
Contrast does not involve task-switching or set-shifting; it isolates sequence planning/maintenance rather than flexibility demands.
Local planning criterion is specific to Tower-type planning tasks (Tower of London/Hanoi); this motor-sequencing contrast does not match the specified planning-task inclusion criteria.
This is not a vigilance/oddball target-detection paradigm and does not reflect maintaining set against interference as defined in the vigilance criteria.
Initiation criterion specifies word-generation/verbal-fluency paradigms; this motor sequencing contrast does not meet that initiation-task definition.
IG-MOV vs EG-MOV contrasts online control of internally- vs externally-guided sequences and shows complexity effects in frontal–parietal networks; meets pooled executive-function inclusion.
Movement-period contrast emphasizes online control and sensory-guided processing rather than maintenance/manipulation during a delay; does not meet working-memory contrast criteria.
Contrast is not an inhibition paradigm (no Go/No-Go or Stroop manipulation); it isolates online control differences instead.
No task-switching or set-shifting contrast is present; the analysis isolates online control for motor sequences, not flexibility.
The planning inclusion criteria require Tower-type planning tasks; this contrast tests online movement control rather than the specified planning paradigm.
This is not a vigilance/oddball task and does not test target-detection or set maintenance under interference.
Initiation criterion is defined for word-generation tasks (verbal fluency); this motor movement contrast does not meet that definition.
IG-PRE vs IG-MOV contrasts planning/maintenance (premovement) vs retrieval/implementation (movement) and shows complexity effects—addresses executive processes and meets pooled inclusion.

This within-IG-period contrast directly contrasts premovement maintenance (delay) with movement (retrieval/implementation), matching delayed-maintenance WM paradigms and reflecting memory-related effects of complexity.
Contrast contrasts premovement vs movement within IG sequences and does not implement an inhibitory-control paradigm (Go/No-Go, Stroop), so it isolates a different domain.
No switching/set-shifting manipulation is present; this analysis isolates planning/maintenance vs execution, not flexibility.
Although conceptually related to planning, the local planning inclusion criteria are specific to Tower-type tasks; the present motor-sequencing contrast does not meet that narrow task definition.
Not a vigilance/oddball paradigm; does not meet vigilance inclusion criteria.
Initiation criterion targets word-generation paradigms; this motor sequencing premovement vs movement contrast does not match that definition.
